title: Alberta separatist leaders pursue different paths back into UCP fold
summary: The United Conservative Party wants to be united once again, but fallout from the referendum is making that difficult.

image.caption: After Albertans voted decisively against another vote on independence, separatist leaders, from left, Chris Scott, Mitch Sylvestre and Jeff Rath are all charting different paths back into the United Conservative Party. (Mantai Chow/CBC, CBC, Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Moving on is hard to do.

A month after Albertans voted decisively to reject the prospect of a future vote on independence, many in the governing United Conservative Party are struggling with how to heal the breach blazed by the separatist sentiment that, polling says, was particularly entrenched in their ranks.

UCP board candidates must sign declaration to abide by Alberta's vote to stay in Canada

blocks.text: The party line is now one of unity. And the party has moved to enforce that, requiring both aspiring board members and leaders of local riding associations to sign a pledge to abide by the results of the referendum, prompting further questions about how unity is actually achieved, and how much disagreement must be embraced, tolerated or stamped out in pursuit of it.

The challenge is personified by the former separatist leaders themselves, several of whom spent months spreading the gospel of an independent Alberta before those dreams were crushed — who now must grapple with their own futures within Alberta’s governing party.

It’s a dilemma that has left Danielle Smith wobbling on a highwire as she tries to keep her party together while the independence movement, never that cohesive to begin with, has begun to turn on itself.

“As a sovereignty-minded individual, I have choices to make,” Chris Scott, founder of a group called Let’s Talk Alberta, told CBC News. He spent months crisscrossing the province in a branded motorhome but, after not getting the result he wanted in October, is now running for a seat on the party’s provincial board.
“Am I going to flog the dead horse for the rest of my life, or am I going to find alignments with those that have disagreed with me?” said Scott.
Chris Scott of the pro-independence group Let's Talk Alberta is seeking a spot on the UCP's provincial board. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Speaking on stage as part of a board candidate forum in Calgary Wednesday night, Scott told the audience that despite his disappointment, he didn’t see a future in trying to rip the party apart or take down the premier. There are plenty of people on both sides who want to strengthen Alberta sovereignty, he added.
“If we can set our emotions aside and start treating each other as what we’re supposed to be, which is one group instead of enemies, we really only can go up from here,” he said.

Two days after the referendum, Smith released a video in which she drew a line in the sand. Hers was not an independence party, and those few who “remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement” were invited to go elsewhere, she said.

items: Q&A: Premier Danielle Smith says she doesn’t need Alberta separatists’ support

blocks.text: The first time he watched the video, he was angry, Scott says. He saw it as the party leader telling those who believed in independence to find a different party. But once he set emotion aside, he watched it again and changed his mind. He concluded that Smith only meant that all members were welcome — but shouldn’t try to seek leadership positions and turn the UCP into a separatist party.

His bid for a board seat is a continuation of what he’s been doing all along, he says, in that he will continue to push for a strong and sovereign Alberta. But he plans to do it in a way that puts independence on ice, at least for now.
In his view, that puts him in compliance with Smith’s directive.

When he received the form sent to board candidates, asking them to respect the referendum, he signed it. He suggests that his fellow travellers in the independence movement who can’t move on aren’t able to see past their own anger.
“Any reasonable person would accept and abide by the outcome of the referendum,” he said. “That’s how democracy works.”
But not all of the separatist figureheads share Scott’s convictions.
Mitch Sylvestre maintains that in his neck of the woods, meaning the farmland and oil country around northeastern Alberta, separatism remains a going concern.

The sporting goods store owner, who helped craft the first petition calling for a separatism referendum, argues that the independence-leaning part of the party helped bring Smith to power, and she won’t stay there without them.
Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, spoke to reporters after the remain side was projected to win in the Alberta referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Unlike Scott, Sylvestre already has a firm perch in the United Conservative Party, as president of the Bonnyville-Cold Lake riding association. He’s one of the presidents who have refused to sign a pledge to respect the results of the referendum and signed his name to public letters calling on the requirement to be dropped.
He intends to stay with the party and continue what he sees as his ongoing educational campaign, but said he couldn’t answer a question about whether that meant pushing for independence.
But he took a less positive view about the calls for unity expressed at the recent meeting of UCP members.
“We’re not the problem,” he told the CBC News, speaking the morning after the Calgary event.
“I’ve been saying forever that we’re going to work within the UCP, but they’re trying to kick us out,” he added. “The unity has to come from their side.”

It would be impossible for Smith to remove all the separatists from the party, given how many there are, says Duane Bratt, a political scientist at Mount Royal University. In the weeks before the vote, polling suggested that slightly more than half of party voters favoured separation.

Instead Smith has appeared to implement a “don’t ask, don’t tell,” policy, Bratt said, citing a phrase first applied to Smith by political blogger David Climenhaga. There are longstanding rumblings about the convictions of some of her MLAs, but she has turned a blind eye to those who haven’t spoken publicly, he said.

But if the challenge for the party is unity, Bratt said, the general public — who showed up to the polls to firmly reject the idea of independence — is going to want to know that their governing party is not a separatist one.

To do that, Smith will likely have to remove a few high profile separatists, Bratt argues. The party has already kicked out Jeff Rath, another high profile separatist whose membership was recently revoked after publicly clashing with Smith over her leadership.
Jeff Rath, the lawyer for the Stay Free Alberta petitioners, says the premier can't ignore Alberta separation anymore. (Emily Fitzpatrick/CBC)

In an email, the party’s executive director told Rath his “words and actions” made clear that he did not support Smith or the party. Rath told CBC News that the party declined to tell him which of his social media posts triggered the move and that leaving the party hadn’t hampered his efforts to remove Smith from leadership.
He also attended the recent UCP meeting and said the unity talk had fallen on deaf ears.
“The people that she wants to unify with, she’s basically told it’s her way or the highway,” he said.
The question now, Bratt said, is whether Rath’s ouster will be enough to convince Albertans that the separatists are no longer in control over the party.
“The question, ultimately, is how many bodies have to be tossed,” he said.
Removing Rath may not be sufficient, he said, and it would be far harder for Smith to remove someone like Sylvestre, who already has standing with the party.
“That’s a challenge for her,” he said.
But as far as Sylvestre is concerned, the demands by, and on, the premier aren’t his concern.

“We’ve had three different premiers in the last 12 years,” he says, alluding to the political turmoil that saw Jim Prentice, Jason Kenney and Smith all take turns as head of an Alberta conservative party.
“Leaders can come and go.”
